For the particular case of the Bernoulli polynomials $B_n(x)$, we investigate their zeros and reveal a novel phenomenon: their zeros exhibit a dual symmetry across two parallel lines, as opposed to the single symmetry line observed in the Bernoulli polynomials' special case.

We establish that for a logical circle group action on a complex vector space V, the elliptic cohomology of CP(V) with the same circle group action can be expressed as the completion of the ring Z[G] with a circle action, multiplied by the coefficient ring UE*([G/W]）。

We've developed a novel approach known as Machine Learning Algebraic Topology (MLAT), which integrates algebraic topological data analysis and machine learning methods. This synergy enables the creation of highly robust and adaptable machine learning models by leveraging the theoretical foundation provided by algebraic topology. The MLAT framework encompasses cutting-edge machine learning techniques, including deep learning, and addresses challenges in scientific research, particularly within particle physics, where topological data structures play a significant role. By combining machine learning and topological data analysis, we aim to provide comprehensive and interpretable models that are both theoretically sound and computationally efficient.

This research focuses on the theoretical analysis of the $J/\psi$'s angular distribution in the context of two specific processes, $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$, with the collider energy set at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. By examining these processes at the next-to-leading order, this research reveals that the former has a negligible non-perturbative contribution, whereas the latter's non-standard processes significantly contribute, accounting for about 20-30% of the total cross-section. Consequently, this research suggests that precise measurements of the $J/\psi$ angular distribution can provide valuable, testable predictions for the existence of the $J^{\prime}/\psi$ and verify the $O(\alpha_s)$ contribution in the $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ process.

This research examines the understanding of Signal PINs among casual and enthusiastic users. Our study involved 50 participants, including 25 signal users and 25 users with no experience in signals. Notably, only 10% of the signal users were classified as enthusiasts, and they were the only group to correctly identify how a signal PIN operates. Furthermore, the majority of the signal users expressed uncertainty about the function of signal PINs, with some believing it's designed for security, while others thought it's intended to block spam. As a result, we discuss several design improvements to the signal PINs interface, including displaying an example of how it's designed, showing how a signal PIN works, and introducing the idea of optional PINs.

To efficiently integrate solar energy produced by photovoltaic panels, researchers have developed an innovative method using Gaussian quadrature. This new technique allows for the estimation of total solar energy with a comparable number of data points as the trapezium rule. The method relies on the definition of specific weights for quadrature, with the weights varying according to the level of solar irradiation at different times. By using Gaussian quadrature for solar energy estimation, the method can accurately track changes in irradiation levels, even in the event of cloud cover or passage.

The success of first-order optimization methods in training deep networks has led to a diminished interest in higher-order methods. This paper presents a curvature access framework for the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix, which is GDN-based and takes into account residual values, in order to accurately approximate the structural aspects of the Generalized Approximate Newton Method (GANN) matrix. Furthermore, a novel GGNN-dens framework is proposed, which efficiently estimates the GDN matrix by leveraging low-rank approximations. The resulting algorithm, ViViT, is capable of training deep networks with GDN sensitivity at a computational cost comparable to AGDN methods, but with GDN accuracy. ViViT is then benchmarked on ImageNet-1K and other datasets, achieving significant improvements in convergence rates and training loss.

This paper examines the impact of grammatical gender on representations of lexical items within multilingual language models. Leveraging a novel metric that quantifies the dependency of lexical representations on grammatical gender, we investigate the representation of distinct lexical categories in German, particularly focusing on gendered and non-gendered nouns. Our investigation encompasses gendered adjectives, which inherently carry gender information, as well as gender-triggering verbs, allowing us to deduce the implicit gender of the accompanying articles. Results reveal that, contrary to the handling of non-gendered nouns, gender-triggering verbs are often represented independently of their object's grammatical gender, likely due to the incorporation of the article's gender information in the verb's representation.

This work focuses on the properties of certain types of arithmetic groups, which are defined as subsets of isometries of specific geometric spaces, where these isometries preserve integer-based algebraic structures and the coefficients of their algebraic structures lie within specific numerical ranges. The main result of this work establishes the existence of a minimum size threshold, beyond which these arithmetic groups become charmable, meaning they contain subgroups with specific desired properties for any given set of subgroups with these subgroups' size exceeding the minimum size threshold. As a specific instance, it is shown that for any given size threshold, there exists a size threshold, beyond which the full isometry group of the geometric space is a completely free structure that can be approximated by another, similar free structure for the given size threshold, where the existence of the minimum size threshold, in this case, is based on the assumption that a certain mathematical problem, specifically Chermak-Daniels, is true. Additionally, it is proven that for the full isometry group of the geometric space, there exists a minimum size threshold, beyond which the group becomes a Chermak-Daniels structure, where the existence of the minimum size threshold, in this case, is based on the assumption that a certain mathematical problem, specifically the Bounded Gap Conjecture, is true for the geometric space, which makes the minimum size threshold, in this case, dependent on the integer-based algebraic structures' properties, where the minimum size threshold,

We introduce an innovative approach to object pose estimation that involves learning and predicting 3D class-level object shapes for unseen objects and categories. This new method leverages large object datasets to train deep shape representations, which predict mesh vertex coordinates. Our complete pipeline for pose estimation predicts a 3D shape and then uses an end-to-end Keypoint-2Q method to predict pose parameters. This represents the first complete system to perform pose estimation requiring only a single training image, as it predicts 3D shape from a single reference image. Our experiments demonstrate that this new method performs state-of-the-art results on the Sun RGB-D dataset and consistently outperforms existing methods for both seen and unseen object categories.

Traffic forecast models are crucial for shaping transportation systems, yet they are often limited to specific areas due to the computational requirements of the models used.
A new model known as ST-Net has been designed specifically for large, sparse traffic datasets. Although it is an improvement over previous methods, it is not capable of analyzing all data points when using large network sections.
To address this, a new feature extraction algorithm called TREF has been developed. TREF uses an efficient method to group traffic data based on the similarity of their patterns.
A large dataset was used to test the effectiveness of TREF by applying it to different network sections and then using the extracted features in ST-Net.
The results show that TREF significantly reduces computation time without affecting forecast accuracy when applied to the full network, making it a useful tool for traffic management.

In the realm of causal inference, a fundamental problem involves understanding how a hypothetical intervention on a graph would affect certain target variables based on which parent variables have also been controlled. The current record-holding solution employs a highly complex model that must be precisely aligned with a hypothetical, intricate causal graph, a task often impractical due to uncertainties in real-world applications. Our work presents a novel family of variational models known as VACA, which requires no corresponding adjustments when a given causal graph undergoes a hypothetical intervention. The VACA family encompasses variational autoencoders capable of inferring latent states and encodings under various causal manipulations without needing explicit knowledge, as well as a simple variant that matches traditional causal effect estimation methods under certain conditions. Through simulations, we demonstrate that VACA significantly outperforms the established solutions.

The Irish LOFAR station hosted the REALTA project, which utilized a custom backend to monitor the sky for radio transients in real-time. Initial data from the 80 MHz to 240 MHz frequency range was analyzed over 108 days of observations. The data was compared with other surveys to determine the sensitivity of the system and the distribution of transients detected. The frequency of transient detections was found to be 1.6 per day within the 30 MHz to 80 MHz frequency range, and the data was used to establish the all-sky distribution of radio transients. The study also examined the energy spectra and pulse morphologies of the detected transients. The research will contribute to the development of a radio frequency alert service for multi-wavelength follow-up observations.

Research in metaphotonics is growing rapidly and its practical applications
are enhanced through clever implementations powered by artificial intelligence.
Our review explores the current state of machine intelligence-driven
metaphotonics by examining how AI contributes to innovations in photonic
crystals, nanophotonics, single-photon devices, and nonlinear photonics.
We highlight how AI-aided methodologies help in analyzing research challenges,
identifying gaps in knowledge, and guiding metaphotonics towards promising
directions influenced by AI capabilities.

The film industry's high-risk nature is characterized by numerous factors,
including box office revenue and critical acclaim. This study aimed to
understand the predictive power of various attributes such as genre,
star power, and reviews on a film's success. A dataset was analyzed
containing over 10,000 films from 1950 to 2020 to uncover relationships
between film characteristics and box office revenue. Notably, genres like
Action and Comedy were found to have distinct preferences for certain
actors, and among film attributes, only film rating emerged as a
significant predictor of box office revenue within each genre.

This research aims to examine the stabilization of voltage under auxiliary frequency regulation in power systems, which prioritizes frequency stability over auxiliary frequency regulation hierarchy, as opposed to traditional strategies. The governing equations for grid-connected renewable energy sources, as per the IEEE 1547-2018 standard, are applied, which include frequency and voltage control, along with DC-bus voltage control. The study considers high penetrations of distributed renewable energy resources, which significantly impact grid frequency and voltage behavior. The stability of the system is evaluated using linear stability analysis and numerical simulations, which demonstrate the latter's effectiveness in enhancing system stability, especially during high PCC voltage dips, which may result in loss of synchronism.

The integration of computing, communication, and electronic systems into physical entities has given rise to a diverse range of cyber-physical devices, which have, in turn, led to the formation of various cyber-physical network types, such as cyber-physical energy networks, robotic networks, vehicle networks, and more. These aggregations pose significant challenges, primarily due to the need for individual networks to synchronize and coordinate their operations. To address these issues, we introduce a novel concept of the cyber-physical network of networks, which encompasses two key aspects: (1) lower-layer interconnectivity, where separate layers of processing, routing, and power distribution are unaligned; (2) upper-layer unconnectedness, where data, control, and power flows remain independent. To mitigate these challenges, we propose a novel approach called NOON, which involves fusing computational and power systems to harmonize the lower layer and interlinking data, control, and power at the upper layer.

Blazars are a subset of active galactic nuclei that display high levels of variability in their emission. This emission typically follows a power-law pattern but also includes significant deviations in specific wavelength ranges. One such anomaly is found in radio-loud blazars, where there is an unexpected increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray emissions. Utilizing realistic, time-varying magnetic field models, researchers applied Monte Carlo techniques to simulate polarization and temporal polarization patterns in external Compton scatters. These models were then used to analyze a radio-loud blazar system and assess the impact of varying magnetic field strength on polarization. Results indicate that such systems can produce significant UV/soft X-ray surplus through the Compton scattering process, with moderate magnetic field strengths yielding maximum polarization levels.

A analytical extension method for atmospheric analysis has been developed, focusing on stable boundary layers (SBL) near complex topographies. Utilizing Monin-Obukhov length and scaling lengths as key variables, an empirical model was generated through regression analysis of in-situ measurements, utilizing data from an advanced mobile analysis platform. This platform is equipped with state-of-the-art instrumentation, enabling high-resolution vertical profiles analysis of wind, temperature, and other atmospheric properties. Measurements were conducted at diverse locations in the Italian Alps, incorporating data from three distinct research stations and two mobile analysis platforms operating at different times and conditions. The resulting model was evaluated using cross-validation techniques, demonstrating its high accuracy for the cross-validation sample set, achieving a coefficient of determination greater than 0.96 for wind speed and greater than 0.9 for temperature. When applied to a new test set, however, the model's accuracy declined, yielding a coefficient of determination less than 0.6 for wind speed and less than 0.3 for temperature. The author attributes this decrease in accuracy to inherent limitations in the data used for model training and the complex nature of the environments analyzed, suggesting that further research is required to refine the model's performance or to adopt alternative modeling approaches.

We suggest an approach for determining if an unknown, pure state exhibits symmetry. This method has a 1-2/3 probability of accurately detecting symmetric states without any error, outperforming previous methods with probabilistic accuracy. Moreover, we've developed a protocol with a 100% certainty level, although it may misidentify non-symmetric states about 2/3 of the time, which also achieves a constant success rate for identifying symmetric states.

Baryon creation is a fundamental aspect of the early universe, and it is a process that is still not fully understood. A quantum-fractionation theory has been developed to explain baryogenesis, which involves the analysis of a specific type of quantum field that emerges from the standard model. This theory has been studied in relation to the formation of filaments, which are essential components of baryogenesis. A new approach has been developed to explain baryon generation in the context of filaments, which involves the analysis of a one-dimensional quantum field. This theory has been applied in simulation experiments, which have successfully replicated the formation of baryons in the context of filaments. These simulations, which have been conducted in various scenarios, have shown that the formation of baryons is a universal process, which has implications for understanding the early universe and its evolution.

As a highly sensitive indicator of the Sun's activity, the travel-time north-south helioseismic tomography reflects the Sun's global magnetic field. It's crucial to consider that solar movements may distort its overall shape, thus potentially causing distortions or anomalies in this key indicator. To investigate this, we employed the travel-time tomography on four magnetically active regions of the Sun, specifically the NOAA AR9214, AR9224, AR9254, and AR9264, and evaluated their contributions to the travel-time measurements. Our analysis, based on the most recent and accurate surface flow maps, reveals that these active regions contribute approximately 0.2 to 0.3 meters per second to the travel-time measurements. Furthermore, we discovered that the contributions from active regions are positively correlated with their mean magnetic flux. It's also been found that when accounting for active regions, the travel-time tomography exhibits a weaker sensitivity to the Sun's dipole field compared to when it doesn't take these movements into consideration.

In the context of inflationary models, a previously unconsidered scenario involves the generation of classical electromagnetic fields that extend beyond the horizon, resulting in an isotropic distribution of high-energy particles. This has led to significant modifications of the background radiation, with an estimated energy density of approximately 10^-10 of the critical density, which can have profound implications for early universe dynamics. To explore this phenomenon, we examine how such electromagnetic energy fluctuations influence the primordial power spectrum of gravitational waves within the frequency range of the Pulsar Timing Array. Considering the most influential quantum corrections, we find that these primordial electromagnetic fluctuations can generate an additional cross-correlation signal, potentially detectable by Pulsar Timing Array experiments.

A new, 4D light field (LF) image format has emerged as a viable alternative to traditional 2D images, offering enhanced capabilities. However, Light Field technology is currently hindered by data storage and transmission constraints, which restrict its broader adoption. In response, practical Light Field image compression has become a critical issue. Most existing compression methods prioritize structural integrity, overlooking display quality. Moreover, previous research has overlooked the critical role of disparity information in Light Field images. In this research, a practical Light Field image compression method utilizing 3D structure is introduced. It involves two stages: initially, an empty space detection module using a neural network identifies and maps disparity regions, allowing non-critical areas to be discarded. Subsequently, an end-to-end compression module utilizing convolutional and residual modules reduces the pixel count in identified disparity regions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in producing high-quality images with significant reductions in both distortion and pixel count.

Achieving accurate cross-lingual information retrieval poses a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with resource-constrained languages. Pre-trained multilingual vector models have significantly simplified this process, yet fully connecting these models across languages can be computationally expensive and time-consuming. This problem can be partially addressed by employing an interactive search strategy, combining approximate and exact searches, but this method still incurs significant delays, especially when performing exact searches. This paper introduces a novel, efficient approach that leverages the advantages of both interactive and non-interactive frameworks, demonstrating its effectiveness through extensive cross-lingual information retrieval experiments across four datasets and four language pairs, which reveals substantial improvements in performance, speed, and scalability.

Design-based statistical techniques can be utilized for precise, cost-effective, and unbiased area estimation in resource-limited settings by integrating existing survey data and reducing the need for additional data collection. Various design-based techniques were applied to a dataset from the 2015 Demographic and Health Survey in Benin to calculate mortality rates across the country's 77 regions and 288 community health districts. Several models-based approaches were also evaluated for comparison. The design-based methods yielded accurate results without systematic bias, whereas some model-based methods exhibited bias. The direct standardization technique demonstrated superior efficiency over other design-based methods, although it was slightly less efficient than model-based Estimation. We suggest implementing standardization or raking techniques for rapid surveys to calculate accurate area estimation.

This study explores the application of classical and quantum Kelly strategies when the return on investment is continuous, with a specific focus on quantum scenarios in both discrete and continuous scenarios.

This study is a comprehensive theoretical examination of the electronic characteristics of the recently synthesized two-dimensional materials, including MoSi$_2$N$_4$, WSi$_2$N$_4$, WP$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$, and MSi$_2$P$_2$N$_4$. We have identified a distinct stacking arrangement in MSi$_2$N$_4$ and MSi$_2$P$_2$N$_4$ that is different from the commonly observed structure of other maateerates. We have also found that MSi$_2$N$_4$ and MSi$_2$P$_2$N$_4$ exhibit similar quasiparticle band arrangements, with an unusual formation where the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) bands cross, unlike other maateerates. We have confirmed that MSi$_2$N$_4$ and MSi$_2$P$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ exhibit excitonic behavior at room temperature.

The transition from a Sigma plus to a proton accompanied by a muon pair has been observed for the first time. Researchers at the LHC examined this reaction in the Sigma plus and proton colliding at an energy of 18.6 GeV. Their analysis revealed a branching ratio and distribution that can be compared to theoretical models. Notably, this discovery aligns with the Standard Model and provides a basis for further exploration in the realm of particle physics.

A comprehensive analysis of a collapsing star-forming core has been conducted using the AMUSE code, focusing on key processes involved in the formation of a protoplanetary disk. Key aspects of the study involved the consideration of magnetic fields and rotational dynamics. Results indicate that a central disk develops independently of an existing disk within a core due to a combination of factors including the effects of disk magnetic field behavior and gravitational forces. In our simulations, these factors led to the creation of a protoplanetary disk within a previously core-based setup featuring a core and disk configuration. In contrast, a core containing only magnetic fields results in a protostar that has a mass exceeding 1 solar mass, with a high magnetic field strength of 100 micro Gauss, and significant jet formation. In our simulations, this mass is significantly higher than in a control setup that does not account for magnetic fields, which results in a lower mass of 0.53 solar masses, with a higher central density. In addition, our results indicate that mass accretion rates are significantly higher than in a control setup, which has significant implications for our understanding of star formation.

The observed variability in brightness of white dwarf stars is often linked to their circumstellar dust atmospheres, which can be explained by the radiation trapping within these atmospheres. By analyzing the observed variability in 11 stars, researchers were able to determine the molecular weight and electron number density of the atmospheres, which in turn allowed them to predict the potential sources of the variability, such as the redistribution of dust following atmospheric changes. However, a constant layer of dust at a certain depth in the atmosphere might be required to stabilize the atmospheric structure, which would help to resolve inconsistencies in the atmospheric models.

This study introduces a comprehensive, multi-period temporal series modeling approach. Traditional methods, which often rely on precise parameterization, may be ill-suited for complex, high-dimensional data. A new, 2018 proposal addressed this by modeling each period individually, which may be effective, but increases the model's parameter count and complexity. To optimize this approach, we've developed a method that leverages sparsity and employs the Bayesian Maximum Staple method for efficient inference of the model's posterior distribution. By utilizing Bayesian Variational Inference, we've enabled this technique to scale to ultra-high dimensional data, which we've successfully tested on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our method, especially in scenarios with multi-period, multi-dimensional data.

A recent finding by Gratz and Podolak can be summarized as follows: every compact Hausdorff abelian group serves as a steadfastness logic duality logic dual to a compacto-reflective structure. We provide additional context for this result, presenting a more straightforward approach that leverages duality theory for compact Hausdorff abelian groups, specifically Pontryagin duality.

Federated learning allows the development of AI algorithms without compromising user data security by utilizing secure communication methods to aggregate local user data.  This concept has led to a growing interest in applying it to mobile and internet services to avoid privacy breaches.  Nonetheless, the current understanding of how federated learning integrates with fairness and differential privacy remains unclear.  This paper aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how model bias occurs in federated settings, how to assess and measure it, and how an algorithm can be designed to address and correct for biased models, while also exploring the integration of differential privacy, its current methods of implementation, and developing a new algorithm to provide equitable and private learning in federated settings.  A comprehensive comparison of existing methods of implementing fairness and privacy in federated settings is also discussed.

A theoretical framework based on supersymmetry and a minimal $U(1)_X$ is proposed with a right-handed neutrino taking on the role of a dark substance. The introduction of the $U(1)_X$ symmetry along with $R$-symmetry in the TeV scale leads to the generation of the observed hierarchy between the superpartner masses and the standard model particles, as well as the dark substance in the GeV to TeV range, by the R-parity violating right-handed neutrino. The R-parity is also naturally conserved by the $U(1)_X$ symmetry. The model's radiative corrections to the Higgs boson mass and decays of supersymmetry particles into the dark substance particle are examined in the context of the supersymmetric mass parameters, and the required R-parity violating parameter is found to be within an acceptable range. The model is also analyzed in the context of dark substance detection through the R-parity violating chargino decay at the Large Hadron Collider and supersymmetry detection via dark substance stripping in the LHC.

This research paper delves into the optimization of a wireless powered wireless network incorporating an intelligent reflecting surface. To address network segmentation issues, a data-driven method has been implemented without relying on precise network parameter knowledge. A substantial dataset was created through Monte-Carlo simulations, reflecting a wide range of potential network states. To address the challenge of reliable network power transfer, a deep learning approach, specifically the U1Net unsupervised learning technique, was utilized to predict the best phase for the IRS. To further enhance performance, the problem of maximizing network throughput was reformulated as a multi-objective task, aiming to simultaneously maximize network throughput and the coverage area of user equipment. To validate the proposed solution, a comparison was made with an ideal scheme that required full network parameter knowledge, as well as with a random phase selection scheme and a scheme relying solely on the closest user equipment to the IRS for phase allocation.

For the first time, researchers have studied the properties of a newly discovered isomer in the $^{186}$Hg nucleus, named $^{186m}$Hg. The study, utilizing a high-resolution gamma-ray spectrometer called GRETINA, along with a special detector setup, allowed the scientists to examine the decay of this isomer in detail. Gamma rays with an energy of 103.7 keV were gamma rays with an energy of 103.7 keV were found in the decay of this isomer and further study showed the isomer has a lifetime of around 3.7 milliseconds. Measured decay products and nuclear states of $^{186}$Hg were found to be in agreement with theoretical predictions.

We've examined a specific theoretical framework that connects two fundamental concepts: the existence of dark energy and the origin of matter's dominance over its antimatter counterpart in the universe. In this analysis, we've found that within our chosen model, the rate of a particular type of particle decay is directly related to the acceleration of the universe, and as a result, particle generation occurs only at certain times - specifically, during a phase of cosmic expansion that is expected to last only briefly. Furthermore, we've found that, under the assumption that particle generation is responsible for the existence of matter, certain relationships between particle masses and the properties of neutrinos must hold true, and we've identified specific neutrino parameters that are consistent with current data and the requirements of particle generation.

We introduce a novel data-driven control approach, applicable to multiple systems with similar dynamics but unknown dynamics and a side information vector that influences system behavior. Our controller's objectives are side-information-dependent, yet we have no prior knowledge of these objectives. Our proposed data-driven control approach can efficiently learn from a single trial, significantly reducing the need for side information diversity. Theoretical guarantees demonstrate that our controller can stabilize all systems achieving the desired objectives, provided the systems are controllable and the input saturation is taken into account. Our numerical results demonstrate the data-driven controller's ability to track target trajectories in two examples, significantly reducing the required side information diversity from 16-wheeled inverted pendulum systems and inverted pendulum systems. Furthermore, our controller exhibits robustness to parameter variations, unmodeled dynamics, and measurement noise, making it a promising solution for controlling complex systems.

A conformal field model, specifically the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda field theory, is developed with the goal of finding new integrable examples within the broader context of Toda theories. We establish a specific conformal field model by establishing unitary renormalization through a well-defined Ward identity method. We then demonstrate the model's novel characteristics, which differentiate it from other related integrable models. We also provide renormalization parameters in four dimensions and show their connection to higher-dimensional conformal couplings in four and six dimensions. We show the specific instance in which this model effectively reduces to the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda field theory. We also introduce generalized twisted versions of this model, and introduce the concept of the twisted KdV model, which is distinct from the standard Witten model, in addition to providing the necessary renormalization in four dimensions. Action recognition in partial sequences of actions relies heavily on how different actions relate to one another, especially in sequences that overlap or are out of order. Current research has made progress in this area, but most methods struggle when dealing with complex action relationships, especially those that involve multiple actions. To address this limitation, we have developed a new approach called Relation GAN, which uses action relationships to improve recognition accuracy. Relation GAN generates action representations and uses them to identify the most likely action sequence. By focusing on the relationships between actions, our method is able to accurately predict actions even in complex videos with multiple people and overlapping actions. Relation GAN has been tested on three datasets, including NTU-RGB+D 50 (split46), HMDB-51, and Kinetics 600, and our results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

A new quantum key distribution method is presented which utilizes phase encoding for phase-modulated coherent states but requires no phase stabilization. The key innovation is the use of different measurement bases by Alice and Bob that are defined by their definitions of specific target states, rather than an encoding scheme. This definition allows them to share the same coherent states but utilize different measurements. This method shares similarities with the BB84 protocol but differs in its more demanding device requirements for Bob, who must possess a more complex device that can generate specific states. This requirement, however, is offset by the advantage of eliminating the need for phase stabilization, thus making it more feasible for practical implementation.

Toeplitz algebras of certain subspaces of the Bergman space, specifically the Hartogs-Ross boundary type, have been shown to be unitarily universally representable. A crucial step in this process involved identifying a specific Toeplitz operator, T(z bar raised to a positive power), and determining its key properties in relation to L2 of the unit disk and the Bergman space. It was found that the Toeplitz operator behaves as a compact perturbation of a projection and preserves the orthogonality between these spaces. Furthermore, the adjoint of the operator can be expressed as the sum of another Toeplitz operator and a Hilbert-Schmidt operator. Building upon previous research by Douglas and Timotin, the Toeplitz operator's behavior on the unit ball in n dimensions was also examined and used to represent the Toeplitz algebra of the shell domain Bn(1,r). The resulting representation is achieved over the Hartogs-Ross boundary, the normed space Bn(1,r), and the unit n-ball.

Detecting objects using large annotated datasets is efficient but impractical in many cases, particularly for numerous categories. To address this challenge, we examine an open-list detection task where the model must identify objects in real-time from an extensive list of potential categories without prior bounding box information. We achieve this by estimating bounding boxes directly from image content, using ground truth as categories in text form. This approach is applied to the image detection task on the COCO dataset and shows better results than supervised methods when handling rare object classes.

The area surrounding the S1 shock in the Rho Ophiuchi region is known for its significant ionized gas shock waves, yet how this shock influences the transition of gas from neutral to ionized states in its path remains unclear. To address this, a new study focused on analyzing how different phases of gas - ionized, atomic, and photodissociation region gas - transition between each other in the Rho Ophiuchi region, using a variety of observational tools. By combining data gathered from several observational tools, researchers found that the ionization front is located at a distance of 1.7 parsecs from the S1 shock, while the shock itself is located at a distance of 1.8 parsecs from the S1 shock, consistent with previous studies. However, a notable discrepancy was found between the positions of the ionization front and the photodissociation region gas, with a distance of 0.5 parsec separating them. Observations of the photodissociation region gas revealed a linear relationship with dust emission data collected at a wavelength of 857 micrometers, and a notable increase in ionization rate was found, with a value of 2.5 times 10^-14 s^-1, resulting in a notable discrepancy of 20 percent between the positions of the ionization front and the photodissociation region gas, consistent with previous studies.

Transformer-based architectures, initially developed for natural language processing tasks, have recently gained significant traction in computer vision domains. These transformers, which rely on the self-attention mechanism, have achieved state-of-the-art results in a range of computer vision problems, such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation. A comprehensive understanding of transformers, including their fundamental principles, is essential for researchers to effectively apply this technology to solve vision problems. This review aims to dissect the key components of transformers, including their self-attention mechanism, positional encoding, and various vision-based variants, such as Vision Transformer (ViT), DeiT, ViT/Reg, CoAt, Transformer-Huber, ViTPlus, ViTPro, and ViTPro2. Additionally, this review delves into pre-training and fine-tuning strategies, as well as discussing the advantages and limitations of transformers, before exploring future research directions for this rapidly evolving field.

This study explores the utilization of factor models to forecast mortality rates, a method underutilized in the field. We examine the distinct characteristics of factor models in contrast to the widely adopted single-factor Coalescent Life Table model. Two novel forecasting approaches based on factor models are introduced - one incorporating time-varying factor loadings and the other utilizing time-invariant factor loadings. We analyze their performance under various scenarios through Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we investigate the impact of varying forecast targets, models, and factor numbers on the accuracy of these factor model-based predictions when applied to real-world data.

Research on neural architecture search with use of reinforcement learning encounters significant issues of interference, potentially compromising the quality and efficiency of discovered architectures.  A novel approach aims to mitigate this problem by examining how interference affects the quality of these architectures.  The method involves manipulating the probability distribution of actions to limit interference during the search, thereby improving the overall performance.  The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments that analyze the impact of interference and provide a strategy for minimizing it.

This research introduces an investigation framework for analyzing time series data through attribute evaluation. The proposed framework assesses specific, computable characteristics of each time series variable. Following examination, statistical tests can be conducted to analyze the differences between groups. The thetS package in time series analysis facilitates the implementation of this framework by enabling users to define and compute attributes that are common, differ only in their calculation methods, or require custom functions. An in-depth look at usage examples in various contexts is provided, including a comparative analysis test using the IRIS dataset and exploration of the Sales dataset from online retail records, demonstrating the identification of meaningful patterns and insights.

We will demonstrate the inner-outer area principle as well as an interior-boundary comparison theorem for geodesically complete CAT(0) areas with non-negative curvature from the bottom, which are confined within the strip 0 <= x <= L and have at least one boundary that appears like a geodesic. This is in line with prior research on general comparison theorems for minimal surfaces in R^3 with non-negative scalar curvature, as conducted by Lee and Ni, or on surfaces in CAT(0) spaces with non-negative curvature, conducted by Lee and Tam.

This research introduces a novel approach to assessing a Bayesian translator's reliability, building upon existing work on combining translation outputs from multiple models. Unlike previous works, which often relied on translation quality assessments for evaluating individual models, our method uniquely leverages actual human translations to evaluate a translator's reliability. By employing a Bayesian framework, our technique estimates a translator's dependability with greater accuracy, accounting for variability in translation quality due to input complexity. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments assessing a translator's translation quality on a real-world dataset, comparing it to established evaluation methods. The results demonstrate that our method effectively captures dependencies between translator reliability and input data, outperforming previous evaluation techniques.

We analyze the dependence of transport and absorption properties on energy within scattering systems. Focusing on a specific eigenchannel approach that involves a complete sum over all initial and final states, we derive general constraints on the properties of these channels and establish relationships with the universal conductance consensus. A specific application of our work to a multi-barrier quantum wire is presented, illustrating how the findings can be experimentally verified.

Deep neural networks, specifically the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture, have been proven effective for image classification tasks, capable of filtering out irrelevant data and retaining only essential information. Comparing fully connected neural networks to CNNs, our study aims to investigate their performance differences by directly comparing them head-to-head. By using a dataset of 1 million MNIST images, we examine three different network architectures: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), locally fully connected neural network (FL), and CNN. CNN is found to outperform the others in terms of accuracy and efficiency, with a notable advantage in training speed and space requirements. These results provide further evidence that CNNs are more effective at extracting relevant features from data, and that locally fully connected neural networks may be more suitable than fully linked ones in certain cases.

In Brazil and Spain, consumers purchase significant numbers of football team betting tickets, which are similar to covered call options. This paper compares the most effective strategies for creating and selling football team betting tickets to the traditional approaches of investing in call options. It compares these strategies based on two criteria: a rational expectation model developed by Bernasconi and the emotional responses of lottery players modeled by Kahneman and Tversky. These emotional responses are explained by prospect theory, which suggests that people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point and are more sensitive to small losses than to gains. Furthermore, the research finds that a well-designed lottery betting ticket can be sold at a higher price than a standard call option with the same payout, which is due to its more effective marketing.

The six-loop value of the anomalous dimension for the spin-dependent composite operator in the O(N) symmetric model is determined to 4-loop order, with significant implications for constructing the global anomalous dimensions table. We find that our 11-loop result aligns with 2-loop findings from Dymarsky, Ismailov, and Timoshenko. At eleven loops, the dependence on the spin S exhibits a spin-dependent dependence with an 11-loop value of 100 N.

Our research focuses on the interplay between electrons and phonons in two-dimensional materials, where novel mechanisms driven by specific phonon modes play a pivotal role. This research is inspired by recent discoveries of distinct electron-phonon interactions, such as phonon-assisted valley splitting in monolayer CrI_3, where a specific phonon mode's polarization dictates whether valley splitting is observed or not. Our study aims to uncover general principles governing these mechanisms and their broader applicability to valley-related phenomena in other two-dimensional materials, including valley Hall effects, valley splitting in direct bandgap materials, and resistivity in indirect bandgap materials. By comparing these mechanisms with conventional electron-phonon scattering, we provide a comprehensive understanding of how a specific phonon mode's properties can lead to distinct electron-phonon interaction mechanisms and their significant implications for valley physics.

The problem of domain adaptation, a key challenge in machine learning, has been successfully tackled in the visual domain through the NeurIPS 2022 Contest on Visual Domain Adaptation. The goal of the contest was to adapt models trained on the source domain (CIFAR100) to evaluate their performance on the target domain (ImageNet) under unsupervised conditions. The contest had a two-part solution, where we developed a simple yet effective baseline solution by augmenting source domain labels with target domain pseudo-labels. The advanced solution combined SVD for dimensionality reduction with self-distillation and supervised self-training techniques. The contest rules allowed for the use of any method to label target domain data post the first submission, leading to the development of the advanced solution. The solutions presented are available for review on the official website and the associated GitHub repository.

A prevalent method in representation learning, autoencoders, typically employ Euclidean distance in their objective function. This choice is mainly due to the lack of supported non-Euclidean distance metrics. This work proposes a novel approach where such a method is applied to data residing on the surface of a sphere by replacing the Euclidean distance with the geodesic distance. Additionally, we propose an efficient target space projection method that can project data onto either a smaller sphere or a hypercube. We test our approach on various datasets and compare it with a leading supervised spherical representation method.

We investigate the properties of the Fermi polaron using an approach that combines diagrammatic Monte Carlo with the self-consistent Born method to analyze the self-energy of a polaronized particle. Our study focuses on a 2D Fermi sea with an unscreened interaction potential有很强的repulsion component and explores how various parameters, such as the s-wave scattering length and the mass disparity between the impurity and the Fermi sea particles, affect the energy of the polaron. We also explore the effects of the higher-order self-energy diagrams to various scattering lengths and identify that these repulsive contributions significantly impact the energy landscape of the polaron. Additionally, we leverage the self-energy data obtained, using the self-consistent Born method, to analyze the width of the polaron's self-energy and discuss how the width and scattering length are interconnected. Moreover, we investigate how the higher-order self-energy diagrams affect the polaron's wave function and discuss how the width and the wave function are interconnected. Our study further explores how the higher-order self-energy diagrams affect the dressing of the impurity, resulting in modifications to the local density of states.

Quantum emulation from the mid-20th century has been a cornerstone in understanding complex fermionic systems, which are hard to study through theoretical methods as well as experimental ones due to their 复杂特性.  Advances in this area have been hindered by issues stemming from mid-circuit errors in current digital quantum computing technology.  A novel digital-analog hybrid approach has been developed to overcome these limitations, which leverages inherent connectivity and a hybrid circuit design inspired by fermionic light cones.  By applying this hybrid strategy to a 20-qubit IBM quantum processor and comparing it with its digital-only counterpart, the success rate of the new quantum analog circuit was significantly improved, which is crucial in bridging the noise barrier for broader applicability of quantum technology.

Given a specific pattern of a monic polynomial, any other monic polynomial with a set of integer coefficients that follows the pattern can be used as a basis for a collection of polynomials. This study aims to analyze the properties of this collection, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_n(\Lambda)$, and derive results regarding a unimodal feature associated with graphs exhibiting a particular structure called tandem-walkable. We also establish a relationship between elements of this collection and those of another collection corresponding to bipartite graphs of walk type $P_n$. Furthermore, this analysis enables us to determine the frequency of particular adjacency spectra in tandem-walkable graphs and establish a lower limit for these multiplicities which, in many cases, is often exact.

A newly defined Riemann surface, referred to as the Hitchin link, arises from the intersection of a Hitchin section and the boundaries of a Teichmuller space, thereby forming a self-contained structure within a Teichmuller space. We specifically investigate an intricate component, termed the Veech arc, which belongs to a particular subgroup, namely the Veech group. On the Veech arc, a distinct structure, referred to as the quasi-periodic orbit graph, emerges. We find that a Riemann surface constructed through the quasi-periodic orbit graph retains a certain inherent symmetry exhibited by the Veech group, thereby becoming a self-contained structure within a Teichmuller space, thereby forming a Veech arc. We further explore the Riemann surfaces associated with a 1/5 and 1/7 twist map, thereby identifying the moduli space and its corresponding Veech group, thereby forming Veech arcs. We find that among these, a particular Veech arc, corresponding to a 1/5 twist map, thereby exhibits an exceptional characteristic, namely the formation of an isolated, self-contained structure within a Teichmuller space, thereby forming a Veech arc.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a significant rise in remote work, with many organizations adopting agile methods nationwide.  However, little is known about how remote work affects agile project outcomes, particularly in software development.  In this research, we aim to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the impact of telecommuting on Scrum-based software development projects.  We employed a mixed methods design, combining a large-scale cross-sectional survey with small-scale case studies.  Our results indicate that Scrum teams working fully remotely tend to have a higher chance of on-time project completion, while working fully in-person yields a higher chance of on-budget project completion.  Additionally, we found that different roles within a Scrum team may have varying levels of success with remote work fully dependent on the team composition.  Through in-depth case studies, we also discovered that remote work can sometimes lead to challenges in communication and collaboration, particularly when team members are working across different time zones.  Overall, our findings suggest that remote work can have both positive and negative effects on Scrum-based software development projects, with outcomes varying based on multiple factors such as the size and composition of the team.
This article provides value ranges for permutation matrices of a specific form and also explores the Gaussian-orbit closure of an arrowhead matrix under the action of two groups.

In heavy-ion collisions, the observation of an ideal fluid by measuring the elliptic flow of light particles has been well established. This study focuses on the elliptic flow of light particles using data from non-tagged and tagger-trigged beauty-hadron decays at the LHC, at a collision energy of 5.02 TeV. The results show that the elliptic flow of beauty-hadron decays is in line with that of beauty-hadrons, and that beauty quarks follow the motion of the medium formed during these collisions. This has been achieved by comparing the elliptic flow of beauty quarks reconstructed from beauty-hadron decays with simulations based on a transport model.

We present a comprehensive approach for computing the homology of chromatic alpha complexes in any number of dimensions. Our method relies on the concept of steadfast homology, leveraging the fact that the complex is a continuous deformation (homotopy equivalent) of point clouds. We have implemented this method in C++ and made the code available on the GitHub repository for chromatic structure packages.

This work investigates the advantage of adaptive power control over a $90$-degree phase-shift, and shows that the maximum gain is roughly proportional to the square root of the number of users in an interference channel, and that this advantage persists in more complex networks with blocked sight lines and in channels with different path loss rates, as well as in networks with the same path loss rate. The proof relies on binary power control and approximately twenty percent randomization, revealing a significant benefit of power control and an unexpected advantage of nonbinary power control. The key findings also apply to interference networks with the same path loss rate.

Formal concept analysis has emerged as a leading technique for data mining and knowledge representation, enabling the automatic extraction of meaningful patterns from data sets. Recent research in this area has primarily focused on understanding the underlying theory and developing methods to generate concepts, as well as the application to knowledge discovery and data compression. Our research, however, centers on the practical application of adaptive formal concept analysis in the context of automated classification, specifically in the field of audit education and decision support systems. We propose an innovative classification approach that combines formal concept analysis with Dempster-Shafer theory to overcome limitations associated with traditional machine learning classifiers. This adaptive classification framework is demonstrated using a dataset containing educational audit data.

This study examines a probabilistic model for point processes, the Strauss model, which is defined by an intensity $\lambda$ and a parameter $\gamma$ within the interval $[0,\infty)$. The focus of this work is on strategies for generating samples from a probabilistic measure within the Strauss model, which are constrained by the need to have finite energy and $\lambda\gamma<\frac{1}{4-e}$. Two distinct approaches are considered, one utilizing intensity $\lambda=1$ and the other $\lambda=2$, with the goal of efficiently generating samples through stitching Poisson processes. The discovered methods yield Mecke densities, which are consistent with the desired probabilistic distribution. The novel technique presented here has applications in statistical analysis, spatial clustering, and computational geometry.

In this paper, we investigate the impact of the generalized uncertainty principle (GUP) on particles obeying both galilean and lorentzian motion laws. Beginning with the wave function's differential equation derived from a linear operator principle within quantum mechanics, we derive the corresponding generalized uncertainty principle based on this formulation. By applying this principle to both non-relativistic and relativistic cases, we obtain two distinct generalized forms. Each form incorporates a quadratic term in momentum for non-relativistic particles or involves $\kappa$ (a GUP parameter) for relativistic particles. Furthermore, these findings challenge the existing literature, revealing a fundamental misunderstanding of the topic.

Timetabling and scheduling problems are combinatorial challenges that have a long history of study, particularly the time-table problem. The time-table problem involves organizing events into distinct periods, with the aim of minimizing conflicts between events. A new variant of the time-table problem is introduced, known as $\text{EPT-table}_k$, which allows for a shared resource of size $k$ to be used to resolve a maximum number of violations. The problem of determining whether a given table can be repaired by a shared resource of size $k$ to result in a time-table without conflicts. The problem is proven to be NP-complete, even when the number of available resources is limited to one, and when the number of conflicts is restricted to a maximum of one. The proof relies on a reduction from the 3-SAT problem. The variant of the problem referred to as $\text{EPT-table}_k^{1}$ is considered, in which each table entry can be resolved by at most one additional resource. The decision version of this problem, which asks if a given table can be repaired using a shared resource of size $k$ to result in a time-table without conflicts, is proven to be NP-complete. The restricted version of the problem, denoted as $\text{EPT-table}_k^{\text{C}}$, in which events are only allowed to be resolved if they are scheduled in a single period, and the decision problem is proven to be NP-complete.
